title: Carbon dioxide sensitivity in hypercapnic pulmonary disease and effects of 6 months of non-invasive ventilation (NIV)
summary:
Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) have major breathing problems. Over time, their lungs and breathing muscles work together less effectively, so the body can no longer exchange air properly. This results in too much carbon dioxide remaining in the blood because exhalation no longer works sufficiently.
To improve this, a special breathing mask called non-invasive ventilation (NIV) is often used. This mask supports the breathing muscles, relieves the "breathing pump," and can help lower the carbon dioxide level in the blood. Many affected individuals then report less shortness of breath, better sleep, and more energy in daily life.
However, it is not yet fully clear how the central breathing control in the brain changes with longer-term treatment using this mask. In particular, it is unclear how sensitively the breathing drive responds to carbon dioxide levels in the blood and how this reaction develops over several months.
In this study, people with COPD who are scheduled to receive a breathing mask (non-invasive ventilation) will be examined multiple times over six months. Measurements will assess how strongly the breathing drive responds to carbon dioxide gas, how quality of life changes, and how often disease flares occur.

interventions.name: The present study is single-center. It is a prospective, non-randomized, interventional longitudinal study.
